strengths: Addresses an important and timely bottleneck in video diffusion transformers (DiTs), specifically the quadratic computational scaling of self-attention over long spatiotemporal sequence lengths.

Proposes a well-motivated Selective Transfer mechanism that formulates layer selection as a continuous relaxation with binary regularization and STE, automatically identifying which layers tolerate linearization best rather than relying on heuristic layer selection.

Introduces Anytime Distribution Matching (ADM), which smartly avoids the substantial overhead of training an auxiliary score-approximator network (as required in standard DMD) by utilizing the multi-step flow model itself to estimate score differences across intermediate timesteps.

Demonstrates strong empirical performance on VBench and VBench-2.0, matching or slightly outperforming dense FlashAttention2 baselines while achieving 1.25–2.00x inference speedup, and achieving up to 15.92x speedup when integrated with few-step distillation (DMD2).
Thorough ablation studies verifying the necessity of layer selection, the annealing regularization term L_reg, and the ADM objective over naive MSE or standard terminal distribution matching.
weaknesses: The evaluation is restricted to a single architecture and relatively small scale (Wan 1.3B). Validating the selective transfer behavior and scalability on larger open models (e.g., Wan 14B or CogVideoX-5B) would significantly strengthen the empirical claims.

The data-free post-training collection procedure is not fully detailed regarding conditional text guidance: generating 50K trajectory pairs requires prompt inputs, but the source and diversity of prompts used for trajectory extraction are not clearly specified.

Realized wall-clock speedup for the base LinVideo model without few-step distillation is relatively modest (around 1.43x for 81 frames), partly because FFN/linear projection layers remain untouched and no specialized GPU kernel is engineered for the linear attention module.

strengths: Important and well-motivated problem: Video Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) incur prohibitive quadratic computational complexity over long spatiotemporal token sequences. Transitioning pre-trained video DMs to linear attention via lightweight, data-free post-training is practically impactful and avoids resource-heavy pre-training from scratch.

Sound and elegant formulation of Anytime Distribution Matching (ADM): Unlike conventional few-step distillation methods (e.g., DMD) that require training an auxiliary multi-step score network at 5–10x additional cost, ADM leverages the multi-step nature of the student flow model to estimate its own score function directly across any timestep, significantly boosting training efficiency and quality.

Principled layer-selection mechanism: Formulating layer selection via a continuous learnable parameter with straight-through estimation and annealing regularization smoothly transitions the model from softmax to linear attention, outperforming manual and heuristic grid-search baselines.

Comprehensive empirical validation: Evaluated against strong sparse attention baselines (SVG, SVG2, DFA, XAttn) on both standard VBench and VBench-2.0, showing minimal quality degradation while providing 1.25–2.00x speedups (and 15.92x when combined with 4-step distillation).
weaknesses: Evaluation is restricted to a single base model: Experiments are exclusively performed on Wan 1.3B. Demonstrating generalizability across larger scales (e.g., Wan 14B, CogVideoX-5B, or HunyuanVideo) would significantly substantiate the universality of the proposed selective transfer and ADM.

Modest practical speedups at default sequence lengths: At standard frame counts, replacing 16 out of 30 layers yields approximately a 1.43x end-to-end acceleration, as FFNs and the remaining dense attention layers remain computational bottlenecks. While the speedup scales to 2.0x on 321 frames, the gain at standard length is relatively incremental.

Self-score estimation dynamics during early training: In Eq. (13), using the student model itself to approximate its score function assumes that the student provides a reliable score field throughout training. A deeper analysis or discussion on the stability of this self-estimation during the initial training phase when linear attention layers are far from converged would improve technical rigor.

Limited qualitative comparison in the main text: Figure 5 presents visual comparisons for only a single prompt. Including additional diverse qualitative examples (e.g., fast motion, complex dynamic scenes) in the main paper would better demonstrate robustness against temporal artifacts.

strengths: The paper addresses a significant and timely problem in video diffusion models: the computational bottleneck of quadratic self-attention under long spatiotemporal sequence lengths, tackling it via an efficient data-free post-training paradigm rather than expensive pretraining from scratch.

The selective transfer mechanism is well-designed; relaxing layer selection with a continuous parameter $r$, paired with a straight-through estimator constraint loss and an annealing binarization regularizer, effectively automates the layer replacement schedule and stabilizes training.

The Anytime Distribution Matching (ADM) objective is technically neat: by matching distributions across intermediate timesteps and showing that under rectified flow the model can estimate its own score function, it eliminates the heavy computational burden of training an auxiliary score approximator (yielding a ~4.4x training speedup over DMD-style objectives).

Comprehensive empirical evaluation on VBench and VBench-2.0 against strong sparse attention baselines (e.g., SVG2, XAttention, DiTFastAttn) confirms that LINVIDEO retains visual fidelity and consistency while achieving genuine latency speedups (1.25–2.00x) and up to 15.92x when combined with 4-step distillation.
weaknesses: The experimental validation is conducted exclusively on a single base model (Wan 1.3B). Evaluating on additional architectures (e.g., CogVideoX or HunyuanVideo) would significantly strengthen the generality of the proposed post-training linearization framework.

The practical speedup at standard video lengths (e.g., 81 frames, 16/30 layers linearized) is somewhat modest (~1.43x), partly because specialized kernel implementations for the Hedgehog linear attention variant were not developed.

The 'data-free' setup needs clearer explanation in the text regarding conditioning: generating 50K sampling trajectory pairs requires text prompts for text-to-video models. It should be clarified whether a text prompt dataset was used or how conditioning signals were handled during the synthetic pair collection.

strengths: The paper addresses a critical and timely bottleneck in video diffusion transformers (DiTs)—the quadratic computational complexity of self-attention over long spatiotemporal sequence lengths—by proposing a data-free post-training framework to selectively linearize attention layers.

The proposed selective transfer framework is well-formulated: framing layer replacement as a differentiable binary classification problem with a target layer constraint (L_con) and an annealing regularization loss (L_reg) provides an elegant, automated alternative to brittle heuristic or manual search.

The anytime distribution matching (ADM) objective is theoretically sound and pragmatic; by leveraging the rectified-flow formulation to directly obtain score estimates from the model itself, it avoids training an expensive auxiliary score network while significantly outperforming naive MSE and standard few-step distribution matching.

Extensive experiments on state-of-the-art open-source video models (Wan 1.3B and Wan 14B) demonstrate solid speedups (1.43–1.71x for 50 steps, up to 20.9x when combined with 4-step DMD2 distillation) while maintaining visual quality and consistency comparable to FlashAttention-2 across VBench and VBench-2.0.

The submission provides thorough ablation studies validating the individual contributions, including layer selection dynamics, the annealing schedule of alpha, choice of target layer count, and comparison against separate score estimator models.
weaknesses: While linear attention is asymptotically O(n) in both compute and memory, the paper lacks explicit empirical profiling of peak GPU memory (VRAM) savings during inference across various sequence lengths and resolutions, which is often a primary bottleneck in video generation deployment.

The framework is described as 'data-free,' but the preparation stage requires pre-collecting 50K full sampling trajectories (81 frames each) from the teacher model and fine-tuning on 32 H100 GPUs for Wan 14B. A clearer discussion of the offline data generation and total training compute overhead relative to training-free sparse attention baselines would give a fairer picture of the deployment trade-offs.

The speedup of LinVideo alone (1.43–1.71x) is somewhat bounded because only roughly half of the layers are converted to linear attention (16/30 and 22/40) to preserve quality. The authors note the absence of a dedicated custom hardware kernel for Hedgehog linear attention, leaving room for uncertainty regarding the maximum achievable latency gains on standard deployment hardware.

strengths: Well-motivated approach addressing the primary scaling bottleneck in modern video Diffusion Transformers (DiTs). By exploring post-training linearization rather than expensive full pre-training, the paper targets a practically significant and high-impact problem.

Technically sound formulation of Selective Transfer: Casting layer replacement as a continuously relaxed parameter with Straight-Through Estimation and an annealing regularization loss ($L_{reg}$) prevents the combinatorial search overhead and minimizes quantization-like rounding collapse.

The proposed Anytime Distribution Matching (ADM) objective is well-justified and elegant. In rectified flow models, using the linearized student model itself to estimate the score function circumvents the costly multi-step critic training required by standard distribution matching (DMD), leading to a 4.4x training speedup and preventing temporal jitter artifacts.

Thorough empirical evaluation on modern, open-source video generative backbones (Wan 1.3B and Wan 14B) across both VBench and VBench-2.0. The method convincingly outperforms existing static and dynamic sparse attention baselines (SVG, SVG2, DFA, XAttention) in visual quality and consistency.
Comprehensive ablation studies analyzing layer selection strategies (selective vs. manual vs. heuristic), the annealing parameter $\alpha$, the target layer count, and loss objectives.
weaknesses: The terminology 'data-free' is somewhat overstated. The method relies on pre-collecting 50,000 trajectory states driven by text prompts sampled from OpenVid-1M. While it does not require access to raw ground-truth training videos, it is effectively prompt-driven synthetic data generation/distillation rather than strictly data-free.

Partial linearization inherits Amdahl's law: because 14/30 or 18/40 layers remain dense quadratic attention, the theoretical asymptotic speedup for much longer sequence lengths remains fundamentally bounded by the remaining quadratic layers.

Attribution of speedup in few-step distillation: The reported 15.9–20.9× acceleration primarily originates from step reduction (50 steps down to 4 steps, which inherently provides ~12.5× speedup) rather than the linear attention mechanism itself. The text should more clearly separate the acceleration achieved purely by linearization from the orthogonal gain of few-step sampling.

Lack of custom kernel benchmarking: As noted by the authors, the linear attention branch does not utilize custom hardware-fused kernels, meaning memory footprint benefits and wall-clock execution profiles at varying token lengths (spatial vs. temporal scaling) are not fully characterized.

strengths: Practical and well-motivated framework: Adapting linear attention to pre-trained high-resolution video diffusion models via post-training avoids expensive full pre-training and addresses the primary computational bottleneck (quadratic scaling with sequence length) in video DiTs.

Methodologically sound selective transfer: Framing layer selection as a constrained, continuous optimization problem with straight-through estimation and annealing regularization allows automatic and smooth discovery of replaceability across layers, outperforming manual and heuristic selection strategies.

Elegant objective formulation (ADM): The anytime distribution matching objective aligns distributions across intermediate timesteps along the rectified flow ODE trajectory. Leveraging the model's self-estimated score function eliminates the costly auxiliary score network required by standard distribution matching distillation, accelerating training by ~4.4×.

Comprehensive empirical validation: Experiments on recent, competitive video foundation models (Wan 1.3B and Wan 14B) on both VBench and VBench-2.0 show that LinVideo consistently outperforms sparse-attention baselines (SVG, SVG2, DFA, XAttention) with negligible degradation relative to dense FlashAttention2.

Effective integration with few-step distillation: The two-stage training scheme (LinVideo followed by DMD2) successfully mitigates distillation collapse, achieving a 15.9–20.9× end-to-end latency reduction with only minor visual degradation.
weaknesses: Limited speedup without distillation: Because 14/30 (Wan 1.3B) and 18/40 (Wan 14B) layers must remain quadratic attention to preserve fidelity, and no specialized fused CUDA kernel is implemented for the Hedgehog linear attention operator, the speedup of the 50-step model is modest (1.43× to 1.71×).

Evaluation limited to a single model family: The empirical evaluation is restricted to the Wan architecture (Wan 1.3B and 14B). Demonstrating applicability across other video DiT families with distinct conditioning or cross-attention structures (e.g., CogVideoX, HunyuanVideo) would strengthen the generalizability claims.

Reliance on automated metrics: The evaluation depends primarily on automated VBench/VBench-2.0 metrics and a few visual snippets. A structured user study or comprehensive human evaluation would provide better assurance regarding fine-grained visual artifacts and motion naturalness.
